narrative: The model estimated your chance of failing the final year at 13%. That means it sees passing as much more likely than failing, but a 13% risk is still not zero, and under the school’s support rule that remaining risk is enough to require remedial courses. The factors that most shaped this estimate were actually protective: they pushed your risk down. The strongest was your record of no past class failures, compared with the average passing student also having none; this was the main reason the estimated risk stayed low. The second was your intention to pursue higher education—every passing student in the comparison group wanted this—and it also worked in your favour. The third was choosing the school because it is close to home; this was less common among passers, but in your case it still lowered risk. So the top influences do not show why you would fail; they show why your predicted risk is only modest. To reduce it further, focus on study time: you study under two hours weekly, while most passers study more. Reduce high going-out and use family support; keep your no-failure record and higher-education goal.
